Outside the Camp
OWT-syd thuh kamp
phrase
From without the camp (Heb 13:13); the place of reproach and of the sin offering, where Christ suffered.

Biblical Definition

Outside the camp—in the Authorized Version, without the camp—is the place of reproach, of uncleanness, and of the sin offering under the law, taken up by the writer to the Hebrews as the place where Christ suffered and where His people are called to follow Him. Under the law, the bodies of the beasts whose blood was brought into the sanctuary for sin were burned without the camp; there too the leper dwelt, and the unclean, and there the condemned were taken to die. So the Hebrews writer reasons: Jesus also, that He might sanctify the people with His own blood, suffered without the gate. He was led outside the city, to the place of the skull, bearing the reproach of the condemned, that His blood might cleanse His people. And the exhortation follows: Let us go forth therefore unto Him without the camp, bearing His reproach—for here we have no continuing city, but seek one to come. To go outside the camp is to leave behind the security, the approval, and the religious establishment of this world, to share the reproach of the crucified Christ, and to count His shame greater riches than the world’s honour. The dictionary honors this phrase as the call to identify with the rejected Christ, to bear the reproach the world heaps on His name, and to seek the city that hath foundations, whose builder and maker is God.

Webster 1828 Definition

The place of reproach and the sin offering, where Christ suffered without the gate; the call to leave the world’s approval and bear His reproach, seeking the city to come.

Modern Corruption

The call outside the camp is softened by a religion that craves the world’s approval; Scripture summons the believer to share the rejected Christ’s reproach.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruption is the instinct, ever present in the church, to soften or evade the call outside the camp—to seek instead the approval, the security, and the honour of the world, to keep a place within its establishment, and to shrink from the reproach of the crucified Christ. A religion that craves the world’s acceptance cannot follow a Lord who was led without the gate to die.

The principle to recover is identification with the rejected Christ. The pattern is set in the law: the bodies of the sin offerings were burned without the camp (Heb 13:11), in the place of uncleanness and reproach; and there Jesus suffered, that He might sanctify His people with His own blood (Heb 13:12). The exhortation follows inescapably: Let us go forth therefore unto Him without the camp, bearing His reproach (Heb 13:13). To follow Christ is to leave the camp of the world’s approval, to count His shame greater riches than its honour, and to seek not a continuing city here but the one to come (Heb 13:14). The reproach of Christ, borne gladly, is the mark of His true people.

Hebrew Roots

From Hebrews 13; the place of reproach and the sin offering, where Christ suffered, and the call to bear His reproach, seeking the city to come.
